# Tooth decay and dental care (`dental_care`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by microorganisms
- Core idea: Teeth are not eaten by a worm. Decay is caused by the soft film of bacteria on the teeth, which turns sugar and starch into acid that dissolves the tooth. Rub the film off every tooth surface and along the gums twice a day with a frayed twig or a small bristle brush, clean between the teeth with thread or a pick, and eat sweet things rarely rather than all day long. Both the frequency and total amount of sugar matter. Fluoride helps enamel resist acid attack. Swelling around a painful tooth calls for urgent dental assessment. A spreading infection can threaten the airway.
- Pitfalls:
  - Tooth powders of brick dust, pumice, crushed shell or acid, which whiten by wearing the enamel away
  - The tooth-worm theory and remedies built on it (henbane smoke)
  - Believing decay is inevitable with age; it follows sugar, and became common in Europe with cheap sugar after 1600
  - Pulling teeth with dirty instruments
- History: mesopotamia: by 1st millennium BC – incantation against the tooth worm (older versions likely); india: c. 7000–5500 BC – drilled teeth at Mehrgarh (Indus region); chewing twigs (neem) prescribed in the classical medical texts; islamic: 7th c. – the miswak chewing stick recommended in prophetic tradition; china: bristle toothbrushes in use by the Song period at the latest; the often-quoted date 1498 is poorly documented; europe: 1728 – Fauchard, Le Chirurgien Dentiste, rejects the tooth worm and blames sugar; c. 1780 Addis sells bristle toothbrushes in London; 1890 W. D. Miller explains decay by acid-forming bacteria; americas: 1945 – water fluoridation trial begins in Grand Rapids, Michigan
- Read:
  - Pierre Fauchard, Le Chirurgien Dentiste, ou Traité des dents (1728)
  - Willoughby D. Miller, The Micro-organisms of the Human Mouth (1890)
  - A. Coppa et al., Early Neolithic tradition of dentistry, Nature (2006)
